The whole thing has no relation to the British North America Act; it has relation only to convenience as between the Dominion, the provinces and the municipalities. Certainly because of the war our obligation became greater; the war was our responsibility, therefore we felt there was greater obligation than there otherwise would have been. Not only did we look after those suffering from the war directly or indirectly; but because of the immensity of the question we went further. Not only did we go further, but hon. gentlemen opposite, not content with the distance we went, assailed us in the countiy for our parsimony and after they got into power passed an order in council going further still. So it is only talking beside the question -worse, it is misleading the people of our country; still worse, it is misleading those whom we have the least right to mislead, those who are suffering and oppressed-to indicate to them that because of constitutional limitations, much as we would like to do so we really cannot help them.
Now, there are other circumstances in which the responsibility of the government may be greater than usual-I mean the federal government; that is to say, when the policy pursued is responsible directly and indirectly for the dire result. But I do not want to be led into a tariff discussion as such, further than to say that responsibility is traced right to the door of this government, traced not by a sleuth of the opposition or of the Tory party but by the premier in the oldest Liberal government, this country ever had. the local government has started an investigation! I have not very much faith in the result of this investigation. I have no objection to its taking place-not at all, and I do nothing to impede it. speechtext:
I
would like in my first remarks to-night to compliment the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth) on the very able address with which he favoured the House this afternoon. I feel that those whom he represents in this chamber are to be congratulated upon the strength and moderation of his remarks. He disclaimed any intention of making a speech. He merely placed the case before the House; but I take it, Mr. Speaker, you are at one with me when I say that very often the plain unvarnished facts of any case are the most powerful speech that can be addressed in regard to it. When the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg began his remarks he, as well as all the other members of this House, were unaware of the despatch which, during the course of the debate, came into the hands of the Prime Minister, to the effect that the government of Nova Scotia had acted along one of the lines indicated by the hon. member, and I would support the view taken by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) that under the circumstances it would be proper and fitting for this debate not to continue. That might have been an attitude accepted by all, but it was not, and there have been some remarks made this afternoon which I would like if possible to answer.
When one is possessed of a single recitation one is likely to offer it when called upon to oblige a social gathering. When one knows only one song one is apt to render it when called upon to help in an evening's entertainment, and the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen), it seems to me, has one panacea and one only, for the ills of the country, no matter whether those ills present themselves in the centre or at the extremities, and that panacea is more taxation and more restriction.
This is his story, this is his song,
Praising protection all the day long.
I always like to listen to the right hon. leader of the opposition, but I cannot congratulate him to-night on his subject matter for a panegyric upon the benefits of protection; because the British Empire Steel Corporation, formerly known as the Dominion Iron and

Miners and Steel Woikers
Steel company, formerly composed of the Dominion Steel Company and the Dominion Coal Company, which separated, and then joined together with stock-mongering manoeuvres too numerous to mention, is perhaps of all others the most striking example of the failure of protection, to bolster up and protect what might have been a sound industry. Because Mr. Speaker, this great industry in the Maritime provinces started with great natural advantages. They had easily accessible resources in coal. They had' iron ore which they were able to bring, from a certain distance it is true, but by water, a cheap means of transportation, from the neighbouring island of Newfoundland. They had the ability, the industry and the character for probity of the people of Nova Scotia to manage the work and to work in the enterprise. These are the great advantages with which they started. But they represented' an industry which has been forced on, beyond a natural pace, and which presents for a quarter of a century the effect of interference with the free course of trade and commerce, combined with the prejudicial effect of government pap and government bolstering up. It is just a quarter of a century since the Dominion Iron and Steel Company obtained a charter from the government of Nova Scotia, and they obtained' a charter which gave them great advantages. First of all, the town in which they were going to start their business was given the right to bonus, to relieve them from the burd'en of taxation, and to give them a free site. I stand corrected if my facts are not as I state them. Hon. members from the Maritime provinces will be able to correct me if I am wrong, but I think I am right when I state they obtained exemption from taxation for a very long term of years.

subtopic: NOVA SCOTIA LABOUR CONDITIONS DISCUSSED ON MOTION TO ADJOURN
speechtext:
Is the hon. gentleman
speaking of the Dominion Coal Company?

subtopic: NOVA SCOTIA LABOUR CONDITIONS DISCUSSED ON MOTION TO ADJOURN
speechtext:
No, the Dominion Steel Company. They obtained exemption from taxation for a very long term of years, and if I mistake not they received a free site for their plant. They were also benefited' in this way, as has been pointed out by the hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock) this afternoon., The government of Nova Scotia owns the resources, as governments should own such great natural resources as coal, and it imposes a reasonable royalty on coal that is mined there. The royalty at that time was 124 cents a ton, but, in favour of this steel company, it was reduced to 61 cents per ton on all the coal mined for the purpose of being used in the production of
steel, or for the bunkering of ships which carried' the steel away from their works Very substantial benefits were thus given to this big enterprise. Not only that, but privileges of more doubtful utility were given to this new company. The directors were given the right to contract with the company because they were very closely interwoven with the Dominion Coal Company, and the new steel company was given the right to pay dividends on its preferred stock while the plant was in course of construction. Anything which could stimulate, which could galvanize this industry into life, was given by the Nova Scotia government. Then the town of Sydney implemented its part in the arrangement, as I have said, by giving a site and exemption from taxation for a number of years.
But that was not sufficient. The Dominion government cast a beneficent eye on this enterprise and it was given assistance. First of all, it was helped by the tariff. To hear the leader of the opposition speak this afternoon, one would have thought that this industry down in Nova Scotia was suffering from the absence of a tariff; but I see that steel billets are protected from $1.50 to $2.50 a ton; rolled iron or steel angles, from $4.25 to 87 a ton; bar iron or steel, rolled, from $4.25 to $7 a ton; rolled iron or steel plate, not less than one-quarter inch thick, from $2 to $3 a ton; rolled iron or steel plates or sheets, not otherwise provided for, from $4.25 to $7 a ton; iron or steel railway bars for railways, from $4.50 to $7 a ton; switches, frogs, crossings and intersections, 20 per cent British preference, 30 per cent intermediate tariff, 324 per cent general tariff; nails, bolts, spikes and so forth, 20 per cent British preference, 30 per cent intermediate tariff and 35 per cent general tariff.
Therefore, the benefits, if benefits there be of a tariff, were given to this industry. But that was not all. It was bonused directly from the state. That was not sufficient. People who wanted to build railways in this country were directed that if they wanted to have the subsidies which the building of railways would entitle them to receive from the government, must buy their rails from rail manufacturers in Canada and that meant either manufacturers at the Sault or manufacturers at Sydney. Therefore, there was no means known to the protectionist mind which was not taken for the purpose of helping on this industry. What was the result? The result was that every favour given by the Canadian people to this industry was capitalized by the promoters or the management by a watering stock, capitalization against the
Miners and Steel Workers

consuming public of Canada. There is no question of that. The leader of the opposition in regard to the watering of stock seemed to have a sneaking view in his mind that probably there had been more or less humidity about the organization and development of this company than there should have been. But, he said, the watering of stock does not have anything to do with the matter. I take issue with my learned and right hon. friend in that regard. It has a great deal to do with the matter. First of all, if an administration pays dividends on watered stock, what is it doing? Nobody wants to deny to capital a fair return. It is a short-sighted policy that wishes to deny to capital a fair return; but if dividends are paid on watered stock, that means merely this, that profits which should go to building up reserves for a rainy day or to labour, are paid to people who have no right to get them
Some months ago I had the pleasure of a conversation with a gentleman who attended the conference at Genoa on behalf of the government as one of its technical advisers. He told me that he had discussed watering of stock with many labour leaders from all parts of the world, and he found them, as a rule, most reasonable men, as convinced as he was himself that capital should be allowed to earn a fair return, but having the conviction that one of the things which keep labour and capital apart, which caused a rankling sense of injustice to be in tire breasts of labour people throughout the world, was this watering of stock, the payment of dividends on fictitious capital. Even when dividends are not paid, it has a bad effect on the company. It destroys the morale of those who are responsible for the company's success. They see supposedly invested in their industry vast amounts of capital on which they cannot earn a dividend, and they are therefore discouraged. It also lends its influence to stock jobbing, to the going up and going down of stock on a stock exchange until the stock becomes a method for gambling, and until honest and prudent investors do not want to touch it at all. That is another effect of the watering of stock and I think it has a great deal to do with the matter.
Another argument advanced by the leader of the opposition was that coal production has gone down. He says: Why?-because iron production has gone down and therefore we want a higher duty on iron. I should like to carry that investigation just one or two steps further. I am not sure whether iron production has gone down or not, but for the purpose of the argument, let us

assume that iron production has gone down. Why has it gone down?-because the demand has gone down. Why has the demand gone down?-because 'the buying power of the people has gone down and if-and this will come in immediately with a further argument which he advanced-by raising prices generally all along the line, you reduce the purchasing power of the people, you will reduce the demand and you will reduce the demand for iron and for coal. If you ask a man to pay more than he should for his boots, his clothes, his hat and all the other things that go into the maintenance of himself and his family, he will not have so much money left to erect a bam that he desires to build, and if he does not build it, the demand for steel, iron or wire nails goes down to that extent. That is the way in which the whole thing happens. The idea that you can get this country into a prosperous condition by increasing the cost of living, by making it more expensive to do business, is about as wise an idea as the one that you can raise yourself by taking a firm grasp of your own boot straps. I would have the House note this. My learned and right hon. friend says that this raising of the duty on iron and coal should not be a thing taken by itself-he spoke similarly in regard to freight rates the other night-it should form part of the structure of a general enhancement of duties. Where does the consumer come in if there is a general enhancement of prices? If you are going to advance the price of iron and coal, then you are going to advance the price of articles which go into the manufacture of nearly everything that is used in this country, and if you do that, you are going to make living in Canada more expensive. We talk about taxation in this country. We do not want to see taxation raised. We are quite right in that. We ought to try to reduce taxes if we possibly can, but to reduce taxes, you must reduce expenditure. There is, however, other means of taxing people than through a direct impost by the government. There is the indirect way by increasing the price of what the people have to buy. If you make living generally more expensive in this country, people will not stay here, they will go where living is less expensive and wages just as high or higher.
I should like to end on this note. For men who, in their heart of hearts, must know better, it is inhuman, it is cruel, to pretend that the lot of these miners and steelworkers can be bettered by raising the cost of living and by increasing taxation. I cannot think of anything more cruel, when one comes to think of it, than to hold out to men who are suffer-

Miners and Steel Workers
ing like these poor miners and steel workers in Nova Scotia, that hope, and to try to place the responsibility upon the failure to apply further a system which twenty-five years has shown in their own special case not to be a success.

speakeroldname: Mr. G. W. KYTE (Cape -Breton South and Richmond):
subtopic: NOVA SCOTIA LABOUR CONDITIONS DISCUSSED ON MOTION TO ADJOURN
speechtext:
With the hon. member for
Brome (Mr. McMaster) I desire to congratulate the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth) upon having brought this subject to the attention of the House. I am especially interested in the matter inasmuch as I represent in this House the const-.tuency concerned, and possibly I have some shreds of local information which may prove more or less valuable in this discussion. Unemployment, I regret to say, was not confined to the island of Cape Breton during the year 1924; it was a world-wide condition. But the unemployment that prevailed throughout Nova Scotia during the year does not by any means exceed other periods of unemployment in that province. The period in which there was the most distress and the greatest unemployment among the steel workers and the coal miners of the island of Cape Breton was in the year 1913-14. That is an historical fact which I am sure no hon. gentleman, having a knowledge of the conditions as they existed at that time, will controvert.

subtopic: NOVA SCOTIA LABOUR CONDITIONS DISCUSSED ON MOTION TO ADJOURN
speechtext: Is it not controverted directly in the memorial signed by Mr. Armstrong?

subtopic: NOVA SCOTIA LABOUR CONDITIONS DISCUSSED ON MOTION TO ADJOURN
speechtext: I have not read the whole memorial.

subtopic: NOVA SCOTIA LABOUR CONDITIONS DISCUSSED ON MOTION TO ADJOURN
speechtext: I read it.

subtopic: NOVA SCOTIA LABOUR CONDITIONS DISCUSSED ON MOTION TO ADJOURN
speechtext: Mr. Armstrong stated that there was great unemployment; perhaps he said that there was more unemployment-

subtopic: NOVA SCOTIA LABOUR CONDITIONS DISCUSSED ON MOTION TO ADJOURN
speechtext: Than ever.

subtopic: NOVA SCOTIA LABOUR CONDITIONS DISCUSSED ON MOTION TO ADJOURN
speechtext:
Perhaps so; but notwithstanding that statement, I repeat the assertion I have made, that the greatest degree of unemployment existed in the years I have mentioned, when we had bread lines and soup kitchens, and when miners were endeavouring to support their families upon employment one or two days a week. In 1914 the world war came and changed labour conditions; it had some advantages in respect of the change it brought about in the condition of the people throughout the industrial centres of Canada. The demand for coal immediately increased enormously. We all remember that the harbour of Halifax and the harbour of Sydney were both filled day by day with
large numbers of warships and transports, so that these places presented the appearance of a great naval review. The transport of munitions and troops brought large numbers of these ships to our shores and they had to be supplied with bunker coal. Then there was the activity in the steel plant arising from the enormous amount of steel required for the various munitions of war. We had good times and prosperous conditions in Nova Scotia from the commencement of the war in 1914 up to 1920. Then again unemployment set in; and it is strange that our Conservative friends, who were in office for ten years and applied the principle of protection which my right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) lauded this afternoon, had not the virtue to prevent unemployment in these centres. In 1921 the government of which the right hon. gentleman was then Prime Minister found it necessary to anticipate the requirements of steel rails for 1922 by giving an order to the steel plant at Sydney for the purpose of providing employment. This was in the fall of 1921, and in 1922, after parliament had met, a delegation came here from Sydney, headed by the mayor of that city, and on which there were representatives of boards of trade and of the Steel Workers' Union. Their purpose in coming to Ottawa was to seek relief for the unemployment conditions existing in Sydney and the collieries at that time. Surely my right hon. friend will not argue that conditions existing in February or March, 1922, were due to the advent of the present government to office a month or so before. Well, the present government relieved the situation by repeating what was done in 1921; that is to say, they gave an order to the steel plant at Sydney which anticipated the requirements of steel rails for the year 1922-23.
I desire to point these things out lest the impression gets abroad that the conditions existing in the mining towns of Nova Scotia to-day, and in connection with the steel plant, are unique, or exceed the conditions of unemployment that prevailed in any previous period of our history. That, I repeat, is not the case. Unfortunately we have had periods of unemployment from 1912-13 down to the present time, and a good deal of criticism has been directed towards the British Empire Steel Corporation. Now let me say that I have no object in representing their side of the controversy; but the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg read a resolution from the town council of Sydney Mines, describing the harrowing conditions that exist there, I think it is only fair that I should point out that in that respect the British Empire Steel
Miners and Steel Workers

Corporation is not entirely to blame. Sydney Mines is situated on the north side of Sydney harbour. For 150 years coal was being mined and shipped from Sydney Mines. Originally the property of the Duke of York, it was afterwards owned by the General Mining Association; and in the course of all those years the mining that had gone on there compelled the men to travel further and further underground and under the sea until it became exceedingly difficult and expensive to reclaim the coal. At the present time the coal mines situated on the north side of Sydney harbour extend some three miles under the sea; they are entirely submarine areas, expensive to work, and it is difficult to carry on the mining operations. The British Empire Steel Corporation has been confronted with very severe competition in the price of bituminous coal in Nova Scotia. It is a fact, as everyone knows, that in the last few years bituminous coal has come from the United States and has been sold in competition with the coal produced from the Nova Scotia mines. If, then, the British Empire Steel Corporation is to keep up the competition which is now so keen, it is surely necessary that it should mine the coal at the lowest possible cost. And that is why there is unemployment in Sydney Mines and in the mining towns on the north side of Sydney harbour. The British Empire Steel Corporation cannot carry on their mining operations at these mines at such a cost as will enable them to compete with the United States coal coming into Canada, so that they have been practically obliged to close down the mines. But there is another side to this picture. If the British Empire Steel Corporation has been obliged to close down its mines on the north side of Sydney harbour, it is a fact at the same time that dn the last year it has expended $3,000,000 in opening and equipping a new mine within the Glace Bay area. This new mine is the largest and most complete coal mine in the world to-day in point of equipment. It is the best equipped mine there is, and I am assured by officials of the British Empire Steel Corporation that the coal produced by that mine can be put on the market at a cost considerably less than the coal produced in the other mines of the company.

subtopic: NOVA SCOTIA LABOUR CONDITIONS DISCUSSED ON MOTION TO ADJOURN
speechtext:
Is that
No. 26?

subtopic: NOVA SCOTIA LABOUR CONDITIONS DISCUSSED ON MOTION TO ADJOURN
speechtext:
I do not remember; I think it is No. IB. It is a new mine; the equipment was completed and the mine opened a few months ago. That is a large sum of money for the British Empire Steel Corporation to
[Mr. Kyte.i
expend on one mine, but they felt it was necessary to do so in order to give continued' employment to those in their service and enable them to sell coal at a price to meet the competition of coal from the United States.
Unfortunately we have had a considerable amount of unrest' in the coal mining areas of Nova Scotia during the last twenty years. It is not for me to say who may be responsible for it; perhaps a little fault might be attributed to both sides. The fact of the matter is that the relations existing between the leaders of the mine workers and the officials of the British Empire Steel Corporation are not as they ought to be, and' I think the Premier of Nova Scotia had that fact in mind when he offered to appoint a commission to inquire into the whole controversy between the two parties. But we can go back a little in our history and ascertain what has been the attitude of our Conservative friends with regard to promoting the steel making industry of Nova Scotia. In 1912, a few months after they came into office, the then government remitted to the Algoma Steel Company duty on 75,000 tons of rails equal to $294,000, which rails were sold' to the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Canadian Pacific Railways. If hon. gentlemen sitting opposite to us had always the desire to build up the great steel industry in that province that they profess to have at the present time, they would not have prevented the Dominion Steel Company from supplying those steel rails by remitting the duty to a rival company. The Algoma Steel Company had all the rail ord'ers that it could handle, but it was not content with that, it was not willing that the Dominion Steel Company should have any part of those rail orders, and it prevailed upon the then government to remit the duty in order that it might import rails from the United' States and sell them in competition with the products of the Dominion Steel Company at Sydney.
The right hon. leader of the opposition spoke of the presence of the Premier of Nova Scotia at the head of the delegation which came here some months ago to interview the government on the coal and steel duties.

subtopic: NOVA SCOTIA LABOUR CONDITIONS DISCUSSED ON MOTION TO ADJOURN
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman give me the year when that duty was remitted? I should like to make some inquiry with regard to it.

subtopic: NOVA SCOTIA LABOUR CONDITIONS DISCUSSED ON MOTION TO ADJOURN
speechtext:
In 1912. The matter was discussed in the House of Commons in the session of 1913. The right hon. gentleman read a portion of the address, delivered by Premier Armstrong on the subject of steel and coal duties when he interviewed the

Miners and, Steel Workers
cabinet last November. I am bound to say that the well-reasoned, courteous and illuminating observations which the right hon. gentleman read from the Nova Scotia premier's address were in very striking contrast to the original portion of his own remarks. The Premier of Nova Scotia is naturally interested in everything that pertains to the welfare of his province. The right hon. gentleman said that Premier Armstrong had stated that there was more unemployment in Nova Scotia at that particular date than there had ever been in the history of the province. Let us assume that that is correct. Well, I would also remind you, Mr. Speaker, that on the very day Premier Armstrong made that statement there were 1,300,000 men unemployed in England, principally steel workers and coal miners. That number is very much larger in proportion than any unemployment figures for Nova Scotia.

subtopic: NOVA SCOTIA LABOUR CONDITIONS DISCUSSED ON MOTION TO ADJOURN
speechtext: Free trade; they are going up in proportion.

subtopic: NOVA SCOTIA LABOUR CONDITIONS DISCUSSED ON MOTION TO ADJOURN
speechtext:
Well, if my hon. friend wants my opinion, I desire to say, the freer the trade the better, and the less unemployment there will be. But why is there unemployment at the Sydney steel plant? We have the same tariff that was current during all the years that our Conservative friends were in office. There is unemployment at Sydney because of the competition which they suffer from the manufacturers of steel in Europe. This competition is due to the depreciated currency. Since the war the Canadian Reconstruction Commission, as they call themselves, have carried on an active propaganda, their cry being: The way to reconstruct Canada after the war is to build up Canadian industry; and in order to build up Canadian industry we must put on more duties-increase the tariff. If increasing the tariff increases the prices of Canadian products to Canadian consumers, the Canadian Reconstruction Commission say: "Be patriotic; buy Canadian goods." Let us see how these gentlemen apply that gospel to themselves. The members of that reconstruction commission are also members of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association. They require steel and iron in their factories. Are they patriotic enough to buy these products from the British Empire Steel Corporation at Sydney? No, Mr. Speaker. They say: Inasmuch as we can buy steel and our other raw products in Europe cheaper than we can buy them at Sydney, we are going to fill our requirements in European markets. It is only up to the great consuming masses of Canada to be patriotic; the spirit of patriotism does
not apply to them. That is the reason why we have had dull times in Sydney. The depression has nothing whatever to do with the tariff; it is the condition of the currency in European countries which enables the friends of the right hon. leader of the opposition to sacrifice Canadian production in their eagerness to take advantage of the lower prices in Europe.
But happily the picture is not as black as it has been painted by the right hon. leader of the opposition or by the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth). I am inclined to think that the right hon. gentleman imported a little bitterness into this debate because he felt it was the last time that he would be able to preach blue ruin to this House in respect of the steel and coal industry of Nova Scotia. I have before me a copy of the Montreal Star of yesterday's date.

subtopic: NOVA SCOTIA LABOUR CONDITIONS DISCUSSED ON MOTION TO ADJOURN
speechtext: What is its name?

subtopic: NOVA SCOTIA LABOUR CONDITIONS DISCUSSED ON MOTION TO ADJOURN
speechtext: The Montreal Star of yesterday's date.

subtopic: NOVA SCOTIA LABOUR CONDITIONS DISCUSSED ON MOTION TO ADJOURN
speechtext: Then it must be all right.

subtopic: NOVA SCOTIA LABOUR CONDITIONS DISCUSSED ON MOTION TO ADJOURN
speechtext:
Well, it is not engaging in
whispers of death at the present time, but in aspirations of life. I find in big headlines the following:
Opening of six hearths will give employment to 1,800 men in March.
Then in smaller capitals we are told:
Blooming mill of British Empire Steel Corporation will begin operations on double shift about March 16, official declares.
The despatch reads:
Sydney, N.S., Feb. 23.-(Canadian Press).-Opening of six additional open hearths, the rolling of a 36,000 ton Canadian National Railway rail order and a concurrent big increase in the operations of the Sydney steel plant were announced here at noon by J. E. McLurg, vice-president of the British Empire Steel Corporation.
The statement says:
" On August 5 last No. 1 blast furnace was blown out and has since been re-lined. The stoves of this furnace were lighted on Saturday last, preparatory to lighting the furnace itself on the 28th instant, and this furnace will begin producing basic iron on March 1. During this month we have been operating six open hearth furnaces, but during the week of March 1 six more open hearth furnaces will be put in operation.
The blooming mill will continue operating on double shift about March 16, and the rail mill begin rolling an order of rails for the Canadian National Railways. This order is for 35,000 tons, not 50,000 as has been
reported.
" The billet mill, bar mill, rod, wire and nail mills will operate on double and single shift intermittently
as required.'*
Miners and Steel Workers

Amplifying his written statement, J. E. McLurg said that it means that 100 per cent production of steel will be under way early in March. Most of this steel will be needed for the rail order. The number of men employed at the plant to-day, exclusive of officials is 1,061 (this would make the total staff on the job something over 1,800).
The expansion of operations forecast in this statement means a marked increase in employment during the next two or three weeks.
There, Mr. Speaker, is a statement of the conditions as they exist in Sydney to-day. They are not the conditions that existed two weeks ago when the resolutions read by the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth) were drafted; they are not the conditions that existed when the articles from the Sydney Post and the Labour Herald in the town of Glace Bay, read to the House during this discussion, were written.

subtopic: NOVA SCOTIA LABOUR CONDITIONS DISCUSSED ON MOTION TO ADJOURN
speechtext: I may say that the telegram that I read was sent to me on Saturday.

subtopic: NOVA SCOTIA LABOUR CONDITIONS DISCUSSED ON MOTION TO ADJOURN

subtopic: NOVA SCOTIA LABOUR CONDITIONS DISCUSSED ON MOTION TO ADJOURN
speechtext: I read the article, or one to the same purport, nearly a week ago. I do not think it is surprising that if the government gives orders for rails there should be some work.

subtopic: NOVA SCOTIA LABOUR CONDITIONS DISCUSSED ON MOTION TO ADJOURN
speechtext: I think the right hon. gentleman is mistaken; he is thinking of a similar despatch he read with regard to. steel plants in Hamilton which are running on double shift.

subtopic: NOVA SCOTIA LABOUR CONDITIONS DISCUSSED ON MOTION TO ADJOURN

Oh, no; that telegram
appeared in the papers a week ago.

subtopic: NOVA SCOTIA LABOUR CONDITIONS DISCUSSED ON MOTION TO ADJOURN
speechtext: Knowing the conditions in Sydney at the present time I accept the statement attributed to Mr. McLurg in this despatch; there is no doubt or question about it. But my right hon. friend and his friends will doubt it, and I question whether they will be very highly elated when they find that the statement made here is true. The question of unemployment, therefore, is about settled so far as Sydney and Glace Bay are concerned. If this despatch is true, and I believe it is; if the steel plant will soon be working on a basis of one hundred per cent production, then there will be employment for every steel worker in the city of Sydney and for every coal miner in the county of Cape Breton. That is the happiest solution of our difficulty, and I think the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg might very well allow the matter to drop with the assurance given in this despatch that unemployment will cease entirely and that the plant will be working full time by the sixteenth of March.

subtopic: NOVA SCOTIA LABOUR CONDITIONS DISCUSSED ON MOTION TO ADJOURN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
the discussion so far has, I think, established a few basic facts: First, that there is acute distress in the Cape Breton district. I took the trouble to wire a friend of mine at Sydney Mines Saturday night in order to get confirmatory evidence as to certain reports I had heard, and I have the following wire from him:
Much distress and suffering in all industrial centres of Cape Breton owing to long continuation of short time at mines and steel plant. Many people unable to get bare necessities of life. Writing.

subtopic: NOVA SCOTIA LABOUR CONDITIONS DISCUSSED ON MOTION TO ADJOURN
speechtext:
No doubt that is true, but
on March 16 there will be no unemployment and no suffering.

subtopic: NOVA SCOTIA LABOUR CONDITIONS DISCUSSED ON MOTION TO ADJOURN
speechtext: For how long?

subtopic: NOVA SCOTIA LABOUR CONDITIONS DISCUSSED ON MOTION TO ADJOURN
speechtext:
May I ask who sent that
wire?

subtopic: NOVA SCOTIA LABOUR CONDITIONS DISCUSSED ON MOTION TO ADJOURN
speechtext:
Yes; this wire comes from the manager of the British Canadian Co-operative Society at Sydney Mines, a man who is respected very highly in the whole district. I hope, Mr. Speaker, that the predictions of the hon. member who spoke last (Mr. Kyte) will be fulfilled. But I desire a little later on to call attention to a condition of affairs down there which would indicate that as things stand at present a permanent solution or settlement of the problem is very far from being within sight.
The second basic fact that I think has been pretty well established in this discussion is this:	Although the propriety of action or
interference on the part of this government might be questioned, its right to act is, I think, not questioned. Certainly I do not think anybody will dispute its right to grant relief, and I hope that we will have a little more light upon the right which this government may have to make an inqury. I shall certainly be very grateful for further information upon this point. Perhaps the Solicitor General (Mr. McMurray) or some other lawyer here might enlighten us.
In the third place I believe it has been pretty well established that the remedy suggested by the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) is vain and foolish. The facts and arguments that have been submitted to this House within the last hour or so should leave scarcely any doubt in the minds of at least the majority of those present that there is no solution in that particular direction. I grant that we might tax the whole people for the benefit of a Cape Breton industry, but is it a sensible policy to put five times as great a tax upon the Canadian people as the subsidy or assistance that will thereby be given to the steel and coal industries in that
i i

Miners and Steel Workers
particular territory? I think it would be very much more sensible, if we determined upon a policy of direct subsidy, to give it to the company outright in the form of a cash payment; and if the necessity can be established I would support such rather than anything in the way of a tariff. As has been pointed out, the tariff method is vicious and mischievous all through. We are simply loading upon the people generally a great burden, and the ultimate result will be disastrous even to the particular industry which it is planned to help, because the demand for its products in Canada will inevitably be curtailed.
I am afraid that what is wrong down there -at least, one thing that is wrong-is of long standing and deep-seated. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock) stated this afternoon that there had been trouble down there for twenty years. I have been amazed and depressed upon reading the Labour Herald, and I think other gentlemen who have at heart the interests of this country cannot but be troubled very much at the evidence of antagonism and hostility that is found in its pages. I am very much afraid that the proposed investigation by the provincial government will get us nowhere. I doubt whether the mine workers will accept it and even if they did accept it I doubt whether they would accept the award made under that proposal, as it is practically compulsory arbitration. I gather from what information I have been able to pick up-and I do not profess to know a great deal of the situation, although I was down there once-that the trouble is too serious and deep seated to be remedied-although it might possibly be helped-by a committee of inquiry. I have in my hand two recent copies of the Labour Herald, and I find this paper filled with charges, some of them I think fairly well substantiated, against Besco. There are letters published here of a very serious character regarding a spy system that apparently has been in operation in the industry for years. I have here also as hon. members can see some of the originals which came from Sydney Mines, with a notation by the spy himself, as follows:
Please show to superintendent, and then destroy.
These are the original reports, Mr. Speaker and many of them have been published, showing a very, very serious state of affairs, which so far as I can see will render this industry wholly unable to compete with any other decently operated industry of a similar kind on the continent Unless this relationship between the management and owners of Besco and the miners can be altered, what hope is there for
the industry? I would like to give hon. members just one sample of the sort of report that is made. This one is dated January 16, 1918, that is seven years ago. We have recent letters of the same kind published in the copies of the Labour Herald which I have already mentioned. Here is a sample of the stuff that is reported by this secret spy agent:
Attended meeting of Local No. 11. President Barrett was at the meeting to-night; his remarks took up most of the time. Hand pick miners made a complaint about the overmen informing them that in future they would not be paid for extra timber, and that they would not put up any timber in working places. Mr. Barrett told them to put up all the timber that they wished if they considered it necessary to protect their lives, and he would see that they would be paid for it. He said, to hell with the cost to the company, that they want safety. Then the men complained about the kind of timber they were getting. The ordinary pit props are about six inches in diameter, but the timber they are getting now are 14 inches to 16 inches in diameter, and the managing committee were instructed to demand 25 cents each for this work. James Smith made a complaint about Walter Donovan, overman on south side; that the other day Mr. Chew, safety first inspector, was down in the mine, and that while on No. 8 landing south he asked the drivers how they were getting on.
An so on and so on. The report is full of this sort of information, which was reported to the company through one of its secret agents. I do not know whether the reports are true or not, but you can imagine what the result is when a system of this sort has been going on for years, and is exposed now, with all the evidence to the miners; and further all the allegations mentioned by the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth) this afternoon as to lobbying, bribery, incompetence, and so forth. What can we hope for, what does my right hon. friend the leader of the apposition (Mr. Meighen) hope for by putting on 9 p.m. a tariff when such a condition of affairs exists internally? I do not think you can touch it by a tariff, subsidy of any kind of special help, if that were advisable. Surely that is not getting at the root of the trouble!
I do not wish to prolong the debate. I wish merely to call attention to a most deplorable and difficult situation that has developed in that district, and I must confess that I do not see any very easy or any very quick way out of the difficulty. I think that perhaps relief ought to be granted. I think that perhaps this government might, if it has the power, make an inquiry; I wish we had more information on that point. If the commission proposed by Premier Armstrong is not accepted, then where are we? We are no further

Miners and Steel Workers
ahead at all, and this "canker," to use the word of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock), is still there polluting and weakening and there is going to be no solution and no remedy until we get to the seat of the trouble.

subtopic: NOVA SCOTIA LABOUR CONDITIONS DISCUSSED ON MOTION TO ADJOURN
speechtext:
Before the question is put, Mr. Speaker, I wish to add a few words to what has been said already on this matter. I wish to join with those who have congratulated the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth) in bringing this matter to the attention of the House, and to give as my excuse for speaking, if one be needed, the fact that I am not wholly sure that the proposals read by the Prime Minister to the House, the alleged despatch from Premier Armstrong of Nova Scotia, will meet the situation at all. Especially will they not meet it in connection with the immediate relief that is necessary.
At the outset let me make it clear that I cannot exonerate myself as one of the members of this House from the responsibility that I feed when I read of distress of this kind. In answer to a remark of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock) on this question, who asked, "When we consider our trusteeship, how can we act?" let me inform him that so far as my trusteeship is concerned I will vote for and support any measure of reasonable relief which this government would now propose, and go back to my constituents feeling satisfied that they will endorse that action. Perhaps hon. members who are accustomed to paying from $75 to $150 a month rent for an apartment in Ottawa might be surprised if I read to them one or two of the pay sheets, of the unfortunate miner in Nova Scotia.

subtopic: NOVA SCOTIA LABOUR CONDITIONS DISCUSSED ON MOTION TO ADJOURN
speechtext: Why not read a few relating to the Alberta mines?

subtopic: NOVA SCOTIA LABOUR CONDITIONS DISCUSSED ON MOTION TO ADJOURN

I will do that if the House wishes me to delay it to do so. But we are dealing with the situation in Nova Scotia at the present time. This pay envelope bears notations as to the number of tons that may be mined by the miner, and the price he receives. We then have the notation showing tons of rock or cap rock the miner may have to move. He is allowed so much for a certain weight, and then is allowed something for timber. After all that is added up you find a small weekly wage, from which must be deducted supplies which are usually bought at the company's stores, rent, which is paid to the company, coal, which is purchased from the company, water, secured from the (Mr. Good.1
company, sanitation charges, and I see attorney charges are put in here, in order to provide a way for the company to get around the Truck Act of Nova Scotia.

speechtext:
Does my hon. friend

Of course, there may be a middle course; there may be an amendment to the letter which the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) read to-day. There is always compromise; and the great trouble not only with the people of Nova Scotia but with hon. gentlemen in this House is that there is not sufficient compromise. If there had been more compromise in Nova Scotia in the last six months on the part both of the men and of the company we should not have the trouble that exists there to-day.
With regard to the coal industry of Nova Scotia, I would point out that the telegram which the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg read to-day comes from Sydney Mines in which I think there are three operating collieries. And these are the people who are looking for relief from this government or from some quarter. But that is a very small proportion of the mining area in the island of Cape Breton. We have, operated by the British Empire Steel Corporation in the island of Cape Breton alone, 26 or 27 collieries, an'1 my hon. friend receives a despatch from the centre asking for relief where there are, I believe, only 3 collieries operating. The other 23 collieries are not mentioned in this despatch at all, and that is a very important point for the House to note. Coming to the other 23 or 24 collieries, I may say that they are all contained in the county of South Cape Breton which I have the honour to represent. I do not say that things are ideal in those 24 collieries; they have never been ideal, and I hope that they will improve in the future. But there is only one particular section of these 24 collieries which to-day actually needs relief, and that embraces No. 2 and No. 9. No. 2 is one of the largest collieries in the world, and it and No. 9 are on the same shaft, the one overlying the other. In that district during the last three months there have been only two or three days work per fortnight.
I had a telegram the other day which the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) read to the House. It was from the Rev. A. M. Macleod and Dr. Sullivan, who were chairman and secretary respectively of a meeting held in Glace Bay to which my hon. friend

Miners and Steel Workers
from Centre Winnipeg has referred. Those people did not ask me to go to the government and seek monetary assistance. They did suggest that the Canadian National Railway management should be approached to give an order for bank coal so that the operators could go ahead and mine it, thus giving employment and helping them out of their difficult position, the railway to take delivery in the spring. They also suggested that I should see the railway management as to a rail order.
I knew that a rail order had been given three or four weeks ago-the order to which reference is made in yesterday's Montreal Star. That is the only source from which I have had complaints since I came to Ottawa this session. I know there is difficulty in the Sydney mines as mentioned in the telegram to my hon. friend (Mr. Woodsworth). The cause of that difficulty has been explained by my colleague from Cape Breton South and Richmond (Mr. Kyte).
As requested, I went down to Montreal last Thursday and saw Mr. Wolvin, president of the British Empire Steel Corporation, and Mr. Vaughan, purchasing agent of the Canadian National Railways. It has been suggested to-night that the Canadian National Railways would not buy bank coal because it deteriorates. Let me say that the Canadian National has been buying and using bank coal for the last twenty-five years. There was, 1 believe, a little difficulty because last year the coal was not mixed with newly mined coal. It must be remembered that it is only in the summer months that we can ship our coal satisfactorily from Cape Breton; in the winter time the railway rates are prohibitive. Those two gentlemen were unable to take action because nobody knows where he is at, to use a colloquial expression. The British Empire Steel Corporation do not know what freight rates they will be charged on their coal. My hon. friend from Bow River (Mr. Garland) suggests that they were asking all the trade could bear. Is my hon. friend so charitably disposed that he would sell his grain to-day for $1.10 a bushel when the market price ranges from $2.00 to $2.05? I presume the British Empire Steel Corporation is in the same good company with my hon. friend in this regard: they get what the trade can bear, and so does he. The Canadian National cannot contract with the British Empire Steel Corporation because the trade is in such an unsettled state; the corporation do not know whether they will be forced to pay ten per cent more than the present rates, or whether they will be allowed by the commission to put into effect a ten per cent reduction. I am in hopes that there will be
no decrease in the miners' wages. I believe that if the miners get steady work they are practically satisfied to continue at their present wages. I repeat, I am in hopes, and those hopes I believe are well founded, that there will be no reduction in the miners' wages, especially in Cape Breton. Those are the only two mines out of twenty-six from which I have had any complaints. Of course, everything is not satisfactory. In the other mines they are only working three and four hours a day. But may I point out to my hon. friend (Mr. Woodsworth) that if he turns over the front page of the Sydney Post from which he read the horrible picture there painted, he will find on the next page a glowing picture from the town of New Waterford, where their four collieries have been working for the last month or more. There are always two sides to every question.
My hon. friend from Brant (Mr. Good) may talk about the spy syktem and so forth, but the trouble originated during the war. Previous to 1914 we never had any difficulty in selling all the coal we could mine in Nova Scotia; we had a splendid market in Montreal and Quebec. At that time the British Empire Steel Corporation-then the Dominion Steel and Iron Company-had a magnificent fleet of coal ships plying between Sydney and Montreal. Those ships, I venture to say, carried coal cheaper than any other transportation line in America. The company also owned well-equipped piers both in Sydney and in Montreal. Soon after the war started practically every one of those ships was commandeered by the British Admiralty, and as a result we lost the Montreal market, which was captured by the Americans. They hold a great part of it still, but we are gradually coming in again and I am hopeful that a few years hence the British Empire Steel Corporation and the other coal companies of Nova Scotia will have completely regained that market.
To show how much a very slight reduction of freight rates will benefit our coal trade, I may mention that through the action of the Minister of Mines (Mr. Stewart) a bonus of one-fifth of a cent per ton per mile was granted by the government last year on all coal from Nova Scotia mines destined for points west of Riviere du Loup. This enabled the British Empire Steel Corporation to ship 100,000 tons of coal to markets which they were never able to reach before. There is one of the difficulties which the coal trade of Nova Scotia has to contend with. We may talk about tariff and other things, but the cost of rail transportation is the great underlying
Miners and Steel Workers

difficulty confronting the coal trade of our province.
The steel industry has been at a low ebb throughout the world for the last year, but we have not been in such very bad condition in Sydney. Some portions of the city are in bad straits, of course, but the first of this year the British Empire Steel Corporation was able to capture a very large share of the Australia and New Zealand markets. When I left Sydney the first of this month a steamer was clearing from the port of Louisburg for Australia laden with products of the Dominion Iron and Steel Company. I do not think the outlook is so very bad. I am hopeful that the proposition put forward by Premier Armstrong will be accepted both by the British Empire Steel Corporation and by the workers, and that they will be able to get to work on their summer contracts in April. If so, I feel that the whole trouble of the coal and steel industry in Nova Scotia will be at an end.
I am not going to argue, Mr. Speaker, whether we had harder times under the Conservative government than we are having under the Liberal government; I am not going to argue that the tariff would or would not be a cure for our troubles in Nova Scotia; but I do say-and I think it was pointed out by my hon. friend from Bow River-that the miners themselves think that the tariff is not going to help them, because when the delegation from that province went to the United Mine Workers and asked them to appoint delegates to go to Ottawa to interview the government in order to obtain an increase of tariff, those mine workers absolutely refused to do so.
The right hon. gentleman speaks about the tariff being the trouble with us. I do not think it is. The tariff on run of mine coal remained at 53 cents a ton from 1911 until 1917 and on slack coal at 14 cents a ton from 1911 until 1921. If my hon. friends on the other side, who were then in power, thought that an increase in the tariff would be beneficial to the coal trade in this country, why did they not put that policy into effect and give us a higher tariff? That is something I am unable to understand.

With regard to some of my hon. friends who seem to think that no good has come out of conciliation boards or out of royal commissions as regards the coal trade, may I say that there has never been a royal commission or a conciliation board dealing with the question of coal in Nova Scotia that did not give the miners of that province an increase? I think under the premiership of the present leader of the opposition a royal commission was sent down to Nova Scotia in the summer of 1917 or 1918, and I remember that Rev. Clarence McKinnon was one of the members of that commission. As a matter of fact it may have been later than that; it may have been in 1919 or 1920. They went down there to investigate the coal industry in Nova Scotia, and without getting the two parties together, without going into the question at all they got the operators to agree to give the men a ten per cent increase. The same result has followed from two or three different concilia-

Miners and Steel Workers

tion boards. I am not going into the question of who should appoint a royal commission to investigate coal conditions in the province of Nova Scotia or any other province, but had Premier Armstrong refused or neglected to appoint a royal commission in this instance, I was prepared to move the adjournment of the House here on some occasion in order to ask this government to appoint a commission of inquiry. But Premier Armstrong has appointed a commission, and there is therefore no necessity for this government to jump in at the present time.
A royal commission was asked for in 1921, I think, and a delegation came up here. At that time I said I was opposed to this government appointing a royal commission until they had found out whether anything could be done und'er the conciliation act. A great deal has been said in the debates this session as to the action of the Privy Council in declaring ultra vires of this parliament the so-called Lemieux Act. May I point out that on the statute books of Nova Scotia there has been since 1890 one of the best arbitration and conciliation acts for the settlement of disputes between employers and employees that exists on the statute books of this country. It is contained in chapter 21 of the old revised statutes of Nova Scotia, 1900. There may be some phases of that arbitration act which do not suit present day conditions, because it has not been brought up to date; but in every instance where trouble has occurred between employer and employee in Nova Scotia we have fallen back on the conciliation act of the federal government. The coal industry in Nova Scotia is not disturbed by the fact that the Privy Council has a'eclared that act ultra vires of this parliament. It is unfortunate that that has happened, but we are not badly off in that respect in Nova Scotia. So far as the province of Nova Scotia is concerned, in order to show you that they intended to look after their poor and distressed, the Assembly of the province twenty-five years ago delegated to the municipalities power to look after their poor and' distressed. I do not pretend to know what the conditions are in other provinces, but obviously twenty-five years ago Nova Scotia intended the municipalities to look after the poor and distressed in that province. I do not say that the time may not come-the time has been in this country -when this government should alleviate the suffering of the poor in any province. There may come a time when that will be necessary; it may be now; it may be that before this parliament rises dire necessity may exist in 
some part of this country which this government should relieve. But I do not think that time has come. There is a board of trad'e in my part of the country, in South Cape Breton, which has asked this government for relief, and those are the only terms upon which I would support this government giving monetary relief to any part of this country, when and only when the parties who are responsible for the relief of the poor should come to this government and ask for help. But not one city board in my county has asked for help. They are doing What they can, and our business men are also contributing to the relief of the poor and unemployed. I do not know just how they are getting along, but I do know that up to the present time not one of our city boards has asked this government to come to their assistance in that regard.
I have taken a little more time than I intended. As a matter of fact, I aid not intend to say anything on this subject at all.

In rising to make a few remarks I can scarcely hope to add any new information on the subject under discussion; nor is it my intention to attempt to criticise to any extent such policies as may have been advanced as a remedial measure for the situation which is reported' to exist in the Nova Scotia mining and steel industrial centres. I rise rather to see whether I cannot bring the matter to some practical head, to see whether, after all the threshing of straw that has continued throughout the day, there may not have been a little golden grain somewhere for those hungry people in Nova Scotia. I have heard it said that while Rome was burning Nero fiddled, and it is just possible that while we have wrangled here in parliament in political gymnastics and spent the whole day discussing constitutional trivialities, there are some children in Nova Scotia starving. So that if there is going to be any point to our discussion, if we are at all justified in occupying the attention of the House for the last six hours, I surely am now justified in making a plea that the government of the day, having recognized the facts in the case before us, will proceed to give some immediate relief to a situation which is stated in the motion as being urgent-something that has to be dealt with immediately. In making my plea for this relief I want first of all to enumerate, the salient facts of the case; I want to recall the attitude of the government as expressed on the issue, to point out the policy that has been advanced by others and repudiated by the government, and to ask if the government is prepared to take some practical action that will relieve the situation.
The hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth) presented the case for the Nova Scotia miners. He has been complimented on his presentation from all parts of the House, so that I gather from that circumstance that he was fair and did not ex-

Miners and Steel Workers
aggerate the facts. Now the facts which I wish to enumerate at the moment, and which are relevant to the plea which I wish to make are that there are distressful conditions existing in Nova Scotia at the present time. These conditions are of long standing but at present have reached unprecedented intensity. These alarming economic conditions which are said to be chronic by the hon. member for Cape Breton South and Richmond (Mr. Kyte), and which are admitted to be very serious at the moment, have been brought about partly by industrial disputes between the men and the company, and partly by very undesirable economic conditions which are not confined to Nova Scotia, but which are widespread throughout the Dominion of Canada, but which seem to have reached a more alarming proportion in that province than in some other provinces.
In connection with this condition an appeal has been brought before this House asking for relief. That appeal was inspired by a message sent by the relief committee of Nova Scotia to the effect that there were a great many people there who were suffering from great distress and were in danger of starvation. We were told by the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth) of some of the conditions that existed there, and I must say that while some of the conditions which he portrayed seemed to me to be almost unbelievable, still I must recall the fact that the hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock) acknowledged that there had been no exaggeration and that the case had been stated very fairly. We hear from the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg that a great number of people were living on meals which cost about four cents each. We hear that some children had no clothing except old flour bags. We hear that some of the children did not perhaps have very good flour bags, and some of them were very hungry; so much so that people had been known to gather mushrooms in the field in order to keep them from starvation. I hope hon. members from Nova Scotia will not think for one moment that I am trying to throw a slur at that province when I mention these facts. I venture to say that to some extent these conditions can be found all over Canada. I think the Minister of Labour possibly has in his possession at the moment a message by the mayor of my own city informing him of the conditions in our city in regard to unemployment and also informing him of the suffering of men and women brought into Calgary this year as a result of the immigration policy of the government. This shows it is not only Nova Scotia alone
fMr. Irvine.]
that is suffering, but it happens at the moment that the conditions are more acute there than anywhere else.
These are the conditions and the question is what can this parliament do. We have not helped the miners of Nova Scotia, nor have we helped the people of that province, nor have we improved the business conditions of the company by the discussion which has taken place to-day. The only way we could expect to improve conditions down there would be by giving some relief to the people actually suffering. What then can we do about that? I turn to see what is the attitude of the government, and in order to find the attitude of the government I must refer to the utterances of the hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock) and of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). The Minister of Labour as already pointed out acknowledged the facts as stated by the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth). He expressed his sympathy for the suffering people and he also added his regrets that such a condition existed. But while he was sympathetic, as I am sure we all are, and while he regretted the situation, as I am sure we all do, he confessed the impotence of the government to do anything in the matter. According to him it was not possible for parliament to take any action in this case. I am very glad Mr. Speaker for one thing at least in this discussion, that the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) has, I hope, forever tom the covering of the British North America Act from the shoulders of the government and exposed the nakedness of their policy to the Dominion of Canada. With regard to labour policies and labour difficulties, ever since I have been in this House, the minister has rolled himself up in the British North America Act. I am glad, I say, to hear that this issue has been completely and finally separated from the British North America Act, at least as regards the plea for relief which I want to make now to this government on behalf of the starving people of Nova Scotia. We are asking for a sympathetic consideration which, as the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) has pointed out, has been granted by this parliament in many instances prior to this. We are told that ninety millions of the people's money, that is ninety million dollars from the pockets of the Canadian people, have been donated to the company that is at the present time largely responsible for the starvation conditions in Nova Scotia. I wish that some British North America Act had stood in the way of those donations.

Miners and Steel Workers

In using the word "donate," I was using it entirely on my own account and was not putting it into the mouth of the Minister of Labour. But you may modify the word, if you wish; you may call it "expenditure" if that sounds better. We have expended ninety million dollars of public money on this company, and I say there was no British North America Act then to stand in the way of that-. If I mistake not, both historic parties have to accept responsibility for that expenditure. Whether that expenditure was justified or not, I am not now discussing; but if the Canadian government has, without hesitation, spent ninety million dollars of the people's money in building up a company, surely we can make a small donation to save from starvation some children that are suffering at the hands of that very company which we have so handsomely bonus ed.
I must express surprise that the Minister of Labour should have deplored the fact that labour men, not only in Nova Scotia, but throughout this country, are so ready to make their appeals to the government for aid. I would warn him that if they receive no better reception than they are likely to receive today, it may be that they will get tired of having hopes in the government and may cease to bring any appeals whatsover to it. Where should they come for relief, but to this government? Has this government not power over the financial institutions of this country which are more than anything else responsible for the conditions which w7e are now discussing? Has this government not full charge of the immigration policy of this country and does it not persist in still bringing in people when it has no work for the people that are here? Has this government not full control over the whole fiscal policy of this country which has an immediate effect on employment and working conditions of the people of Canada? Then, shall the labour men who may be the victims of any one of these policies of the government, not make their appeal to this government? Where else would the Minister of Labour have them go? Would he suggest that they lose all hope in this government of interfering in their interests and take direct or industrial or some other kind of action? If the Minister of Labour
is not prepared to listen to their plea, it seems to me there is no other action for them to take than some such action as he would characterize as unconstitutional. It must not be forgotten that even this government found no act to stand in its way when it wanted to find some steps that would lead to the sending of troops to fight labour men when they made their appeals. I hope that the situation which we are discussing now will not be permitted by the present administration to go on until it is necessary to spend more money in sending troops to quell disturbances than it would to keep these people from starving at the present time.

I know my hon. friend
does not want to be unfair, and he will, therefore, admit that troops, whenever sent, were requisitioned in accordance with the law.

I am not toung to place
any blame on the present government in the sense that they did something that was illegal. I simply said that they did not try to look for any British North America Act to stand between them and that kind of action, but they are looking for a British North America Act to stand between them and the taking of relief measures in regard to the miners of Nova Scotia. That, I think, is a fair criticism from the facts.
The Prime Minister, speaking also for the government, brought forward a document which came over the Associated Press wires, I believe, purporting to be a proposal advanced by the Premier of Nova Scotia. On the grounds of that the Prime Minister expressed the opinion that the discussion might very well be dropped in this parliament. I do not know whether it would be in order to discuss that proposal, for it may well be that a discussion of it here might stand in the way of the use that it might otherwise be. I will, therefore, say very little about it beyond remarking that it is too remote to be of immediate assistance in a situation that is termed as urgent; there was not anything in the document read by the Prime Minister which I did not read in the proposal which came to me this morning in the shape of the Besco Bulletin which was the actual proposal of the company itself; and further there was in that document a clause which I do not think any group of organized labour anywhere could possibly accept, so with these observations with regard to that, I cannot see how this parliament, after having discussed this question for a day, can presume to drop it on

the grounds that the document presented holds a solution for the problem of the people of Nova Scotia that are represented as in a condition of starvation.

What clause does the
hon. member refer to as necessarily unacceptable?

subtopic: NOVA SCOTIA LABOUR CONDITIONS DISCUSSED ON MOTION TO ADJOURN
speechtext:
The clause which makes
binding upon the labour men to accept the wage scale which might be decided upon by a committee that has not yet been appointed.

That is, if they freely
