speechtext:
Certainly, but I am pointing out that they are not likely to go into it. If, however, they do, it is not an immediate thing. The Prime Minister also was very careful to throw from his shoulders the responsibility in this matter of granting relief and pointed out to us that local governments must be responsible for unemployment and all suffering that arises therefrom. Let me add in that connection that it is just possible that unemployment and suffering which result from the policy of the present administration may, some day, become such a burden on local governments that they may not only not be able to carry it, but rebel against it, and consequently the solicitous care expressed by the Prime Minister to protect the British North America Act may become the means of its final overthrow.
I do not think that we can possibly hope to get anywhere by trying to throw the responsibility on the shoulders of somebody else. The leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) brought forward his policy; and let me emphasize the fact that it was a policy. It is not my business to criticise it at the moment, although some hon. members have felt it their duty to do so. But at any rate the right hon. gentleman did have a policy which in his opinion would have some effect on the situation. But the government so far has advanced no policy at alL It is true that the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) took the leader of the opposition to task and refuted his arguments in the orthodox free trade manner. And he did it well. If he meant to contribute anything to the discussion, he meant inferentially that the cure for the Nova Scotia difficulty lies, not by any means in the raising of the tariff but rather in a lowering of it. But I notice that he did not speak for the government in that regard, for the government made no response to indicate their willingness to lower the tariff to meet the demands of the hon. member for Brome. So far as advancing a policy is con-

cemed, however, to meet the immediate situation or to meet any situation in a more remote period, the government if it has a policy has been quite silent on the matter. True, the hon. member for Brome emphasized the point that watered stock, which seems to have increased in great volume in the case of Besco, has a definite connection with the present situation there. But I should like to refer that problem back to the hon. member for Brome and I would ask him to use his influence as a good Liberal with the provincial government in Nova Scotia, which is also Liberal, in an endeavour to induce them to bring in legislation as speedily as they can to make it impossible for watered stock to remain in the stock of any company. That would, perhaps, be a step in the direction of a partial remedy.
Now, there are two things to be done. The first is immediate relief in the way of a donation, or a subsidy or an expenditure, or whatever the Minister of Labour chooses to call it. At any rate, some form of concrete assistance can be given to the people that are suffering. I believe that the hon. member for Cape Breton South and Richmond (Mr. Kyte) prophesied that by the middle of March, I think he said the 16th, the whole trouble in Nova Scotia would be overcome for good, and all, although he did tell us in his introductory remarks that the situation was of very long standing and had almost become chronic. Well, if he is so sure in his prophecy, which he makes on the strength of an announcement in a newspaper that he would not have quoted a year ago with any degree of authority, that by March 16 there will be no trouble nor hunger any longer in Nova Scotia, then I want to ask the government, on the strength of that prophecy, added to somewhat by the optimistic expressions of the hon. member who has just taken his seat, whether they will not guarantee that no child shall die of starvation in Nova Scotia nor suffer from cold between now and that date, when the panacea which the hon. member for Cape Breton South and Richmond advances will be put into operation. That is surely a very reasonable demand, and there is not a voter in Canada who would object to anything of the kind; nor is there any British North America Act which would be broken if the government took such an attitude. I have already mentioned the fact that the government of Canada, having made such enormous donations in times past to this company could not very well hesitate to make an expenditure now on these people Who are the victims of that company in need.

Miners and Steel Workers
It may be said that if the government made advances in relief of the miners of Nova Scotia they would be asked to do the same for people in other provinces. Very well. If that is so the government will have to meet the situation; they will have to reap the fruits of their lack of policy with regard to the industrial conditions of Canada When all is said and done, the fact is that the economic conditions in this country account for such a situation as this, and to the lack of policy of this government in meeting those economic conditions must be attributed the present state of affairs. There is no amount of argument, no amount of prophecy, no length of debating,, that can brush aside that point. What is required in Nova Scotia is *what we need in Alberta and in British Columbia and in all the other provinces as well: it is purchasing power. That is what we are asking for, and the government has lost its control over purchasing power by its own action; it has placed the control of purchasing power in the hands of financiers. So that the government must now reap the fruits of its policy. They are bitter and numerous, and they are to be found throughout the whole country; and merely to rise and say that there were hungry people in Nova Scotia in 1908 or in some other year does not get away from the situation. Even if I could take the prophecy of my hon. friend with any degree of confidence, would he be prepared to guarantee that no person will suffer from hunger or from cold from now until March 16? Would that hon. gentleman be willing to live on four-cent meals from now until that time, or without any meals at all? Here, frankly, is a situation from which, it seems to me, we have so far vied with one another in our endeavour to etep aside. I have noticed a tendency on both sides of the House to try to get away from responsibility and to try to blame somebody else for industrial conditions in Nova Scotia. I do not care who is going to evade the blame, but I certainly am anxious that something definite shall be done at the- present time. I therefore conclude my remarks by urging the Prime Minister to give some assurance to this parliament before this matter is finally dealt with, and some assurance to the distressed people of Nova Scotia, that this government will see to it that no one shall actually starve in that province between now and the time when this document, which it is said contains the solution of the difficulty, shall have demonstrated to Canada whether or not it can meet the situation.

speakeroldname: Mr. F. L. KELLY (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
subtopic: NOVA SCOTIA LABOUR CONDITIONS DISCUSSED ON MOTION TO ADJOURN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had determined not to take part in this debate, but in view of the telegram read by the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woods-worth), as representing the constituency of North Cape Breton I think it is only right that I should add a word or two to the discussion. The telegram is rather a surprise to me, because when I left home about ten days ago there were no such conditions obtaining as we have had described to-night. In fact the collieries in that section during the three months preceding my departure had been busier than for any winter during the last six or seven years. I know there are hardships, especially in the coal district of Sj'dney Mines. Unfortunately last year it became the painful duty of the British Empire Steel Corporation to close one of their collieries in that district because it could be no longer worked at a .profit on account of economic conditions then prevailing. Consequently eight or nine hundred men became idle and had to be absorbed by the other two collieries still operating in the locality. When I left the district early in February one colliery was working a little over half time, and the other colliery was working only one day a week. At one colliery there was a loading machine for loading the coal into box cars for transportation to winter customers, but the absence of such a machine at the other colliery virtually closed it down.
I would only too gladly welcome the sending of relief to Cape Breton if the government could consistently see the way to do so. In fact conditions all over the colliery area, as I pointed out a year ago in my maiden speech, are chaotic, and at that time I suggested ways and means by which conditions could be bettered. At that time it was understood that a coking scheme was to be put into operation that would give us a better market for our Cape Breton coal. The rate subvention on our .coal west of Montreal helped us to extend our market. We asked for other assistance to improve the Cape Breton and Nova Scotia coal industry, but as yet this further assistance has not been granted to us. The difference between prosperity and the lack of it in the coal industry is dependent on the extra market for a million tons of coal. When such a market is secured the company will be able to operate their mines at nearly full time, thus giving the men steady work and full pay, and this will materially help to settle the present unrest.
Miners and Steel Workers

I was surprised when I heard the hon. member for East Calgary (Mr. Irvine) cast doubt upon the outcome of the proposal made by the Premier of Nova Scotia to settle the differences between the employees and the operators. I think it ill became the hon. member to make such a gloomy forecast. There has been too much of this gospel preached in the coal fields of Cape Breton and Nova Scotia, and it is largely responsible for the evil conditions existing there to-day. Labour, when unagitated, has no wish to be tearing down its employers. I give the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg credit for his very fair presentment of the men's case. There are a thousand contributing causes that make it hard for the operator to successfully mine coal in Nova Scotia, and particularly in the Cape Breton district. These mines, as has been already stated, have been operated for a long time, and now extend to a great distance under the sea, which makes it very costly to bring the coal to the surface. Having to win the coal against the grain, it all falls away from the miner, and worse than all, for every ton of coal taken out they must also take out six tons of water.
I should be delighted if the House could devise some way of helping coal production in Cape Breton. One method, it seems to me, would be to extend the rate subvention over a period of five years, so the company will have a solid basis upon which to formulate their plans for securing wider markets for their coal. And when the government puts the coking scheme into effect, this will still further assist us. We have suggested having the duty on slack coal levelled up with that on round coal. It is apparent to everybody that round coal is being brought in from the United States and mixed with slack coal to the great detriment of our coal industry. Some reasonable means can surely be devised to put an end to this circumvention of the spirit of our tariff law.
If hon. members knew the conditions at Sydney Mines from the company's standpoint, they would not be surprised at the mines being idle at this time of the year. This is simply because we have no way of getting our coal out in the winter time to supply the central Canada market, for the freight rate from Sydney to Montreal is $3.60 a ton, against 50 cents a ton in the summer time. Consequently as soon as winter comes on the operators must of necessity curtail their operations. At the present time there are 25,750 tons of coal on bank from last year at Sydney Mines. This coal deteriorates very quickly when it is thus exposed to the weather. Every ton of coal which the British Empire 
Steel Corporation places on bank in the winter means a dead loss of from seventy-five cents to a dollar, besides the deterioration of the coal itself. Nobody wants bank coal. When the controversy began a year ago between the men and the operators, the operators asked the men to take a wage reduction during the winter on coal that had to be banked. Disinterested people thought this a very reasonable proposition, but it unfortunately did not appeal sufficiently to the spokesmen of the miners. The operators came to the conclusion that under these conditions they had not much encouragement to bank coal and lose 75 cents a ton on it. I am telling this only because some members may not know what is going on in connection with coal mining in Cape Breton, and in view also of the exaggerated remarks which have been made in the House to-night about the prices charged for coal by the British Empire Steel Corporation in Halifax and some other places. The British Empire Steel Corporation have no control of the price of coal in Halifax. They sell their coal at the wharf at Sydney harbour for $6 a ton and anybody who wants to import coal and deal in it commercially can buy it at Sydney at that price and send it to Halifax either by steamer or by sailing vessel at a rate of from 75 cents to II a ton. Any excess profit on that coal at Halifax is made not by the British Empire Steel Corporation but by the middlemen who keep the price of coal up. It is not right that anyone should be deceived by statements made in this House which are not true. I would not have taken any part in the debate-the subject has already been covered from every angle-had I not heard the hon. member for East Calgary (Mr. Irvine) making a forecast of what was going to happen in respect of the well-intentioned proposal of Premier Armstrong. It was really a species of inciting the reasonable miners not to meet the operators and have a conference and endeavour to have the difficulty settled as it should be settled in an amicable spirit on both sides of a long-standing difficulty.
Motion (Mr. Woodsworth) withdrawn.

subtopic: FURTHER TREATIES SIGNED AT WASHINGTON

speechtext: On the notice of motion being called for the approval of a certain treaty between the Dominion of Canada and the United States- Hon. Mr. Copp:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: FURTHER TREATIES SIGNED AT WASHINGTON
speechtext:
I would like this motion

Supply-Customs
and the following one to stand until the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) returns. However, this might be a convenient moment to intimate to the House that two additional treaties were signed to-day at Washington by the Minister of Justice on behalf of Canada and by Secretary of State Hughes on behalf of the United States. The first is to define more accurately at certain points and to complete the international boundary between the United States and Canada. The second regulates the level of the lake of the Woods in order to secure to both countries the most advantageous use of the waters therein and of the' waters flowing into and from the Lake on each side of the boundary. This last treaty is based on the recommendations made by the International Joint Commission on the reference concerning the lake of the Woods submitted to it by both governments. The treaties will be tabled as soon as the Minister of Justice returns.
On the Orders of the Day:
Have any plans been formulated for the further consideration of Dr. Tory's report on rural credits?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. ROBB (Acting Minister of Finance):
speechtext: No. I am awaiting some further correspondence from Dr. Tory.
Would the government care to give any information as to when the report is expected?
No, I could not give my hon. friend that information to-night. I will look into the files to-morrow morning and will try to let him know something about it to-morrow.
On the Orders of the Day:

I
would like to ask the Prime Minister if he has any report from the conference between the heads of the two railway companies in Canada with regard to the building of the proposed railway into the Peace River?
Hon. GEORGE P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals): I may say that I have information which leads me to believe that some communication will come to me in a very few days concerning that matter.

Hon. .J. A. ROBB (Acting Minister of Finance) moved that the House go into committee of Supply.

It is almost
eleven o'clock. What does my right hon. friend intend to do?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: We would like to make a little headway. It was announced last night that we would go on with the estimates of the Department of Customs this evening, and I think we might devote a short time to them.
Have the estimates of the Customs department been already before the committee?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No, and that is one of the reasons we are anxious to go on to-night. If we do not take them up tonight we shall not be able to go on with them this week.
Motion agreed to and the House went into committee of Supply, Mr. Gordon in the chair.
Civil government-Customs and Excise, salaries, $585,755; contingencies, $48,000.

(Minister of Customs and Excise): The estimates are the same as last year except that on account of the increase of the work and the various taxes that we have to collect we have found it necessary to add a junior departmental solicitor. That is the only change.
Does this cover the cost of the income tax department?
No, the fusion has not yet been completed. It is engaging the attention of the department.

I suggest to the minister that there should not be a fusion of the costs of the collection of faxes which are entirely different in their character. It is necessary for the House to know what the costs of the collection of indirect taxes are on the one hand and of direct taxes on the other. I am not now discussing the question of the minister using in any way he proposes the staffs of either department, but if we are to know where we are, if we are to know whether a tax conforms to the general principle which should govern all taxation, namely, that the cost of collection should not exceed the amount of revenue from the tax, then there should be a separation of the costs of collection. I do not want to detain the minister, but I would like him to give his view- affirmatively, I hope-on that point.

The only thing I can give my hon. friend now is the percentage of the cost of collection of the revenue so far as customs and excise are concerned. I do not
Supply-Customs

think we have made any distinction as between excise and customs. They come under the same head; the same officers perform duties in both branches of the department. For 1923-1924 the revenue for customs and excise was $298,721,419.55, and the expenditure $7,435,931.59, or a percentage of 2.49. As to the income tax, I cannot say. As I have told my hon. friend, we are trying to bring these tax collecting branches under the one head, and although there has been no change made so far, it is contemplated that when the changes are made an economy will beeffected. For instance, if we can get all the income tax officers in the same building with the customs and excise officers, rent will be saved and the overhead be less. The plan-I will not call it a fusion-of bringing together all the collecting branches of the department so far as that is possible has not been completed yet, but is still under consideration.

I do not want to unduly press my hon. friend. I am going to ask him, however to remember one fact when he is considering the bringing together of the different branches under one roof and saving overhead. That, of course, is a very good thing. But it would be a very wrong thing, and something which would work against the efficiency of his own department, if there was no check kept at all of the expenses of operating the different branches. I forget now what was the exact cost of collection of the income tax, my hon. friend will know that better than I do, but my impression is that it cost a trifle under 2 per cent to collect the tax. We were not then in as expensive a building as the department is in now, and it may be costing a little more today. I think my hon. friend will agree with me, when he comes to do it, that if there is one thing that ought to be done it is to let the country know what the cost of these services is. The country cannot know that if the cost of collection of customs and of excise, indirect taxes, is mixed up with the collection of the income tax, which is peculiarly a direct tax. I think my hon. friend has the point all right, and I am going to ask him to bear it in mind.

I cannot give the cost of collection of the income tax, because I have not the figures. It is very difficult to separate the cost of collection of customs from excise because the same officers are performing the two duties; that was the object of the fusion. The total cost of collection of customs and excise for 1923-1924 was 2.49 per cent. I

understand that my hon. friend wants us to keep the income tax separate.

The cost of
collection, that is all.
That is a matter I suppose that will be discussed when we come to reorganize.

There is apparently an
error here. The resolution on page 8 reads exactly the same as last year, but the details on pages 73 and 74 show an increase of about $12,000. It is either a misprint, or one or the other is wrong.
The amount is exactly the same as last year, but on account of men having been let out at their maximum salary and ne.w men coming in at a lower salary, a saving has been effected of $11,425.
Are there any cases here of the same man getting two remunerations, perhaps under a different name? That is the usual way it is done.
No.

I do not know
if this is the time the minister would like to do this or not, but in connection with all the civil government votes, while on the one hand we know what it costs to run the
11	p.m. different departments, that information is really not correct unless we know the amount of superannuation that is also being paid on account of retirements under the act of last year. In other words, it would be quite easy for example to retire twenty or thirty or forty employees, at a great cost to the state, while making an apparent saving in the cost of running the department, through taking on others at lower salaries. We are really not in a position to know how we stand unless we know what the retirements are and the charges on the superannuation fund.

Of course, the amounts
paid for superannuation and retiring allowances do not come under our department, but under the Department of Finance. Those pensions are paid by virtue of the statute.
I fully agree.
The department recommends the retirements, but no books are kept for that purpose.

My hon. friend does not quite get my point. I am not saying for one minute that it is a charge against his department, but these retirements are a charge

Supply-Customs
against the taxpayer; the taxpayer has to pay the cost. Superannuation is granted on the recommendation of the accredited minister of the department from which the employee is retired, and every department had, and I think to-day 'has a list of every retirement that it recommends. I do not think there is any doubt about that. I do not want to bother my hon. friend about that now, but I think we ought to have that information in connection with all of these votes. I think the members of the government without any trouble will agree that that information could be given.

I understand my hon.
friend wants a list of all these superannuated or retired under the Calder Act during the fiscal year.
With the amount of salary in each case.
I will bring that down.

I have already been trying to get that very information, but I was told by the Civil Service Commission, I think, that some of the departments had not turned in a report to them. I think the government ought to give a complete list to the House of all these retirements and superannuations from all departments during the year, and it would be far better if the whole list were tabled at one time than to worry each minister for a statement.
There should not be any trouble getting the information from the Civil Service Commission. The commission recommends all these retirements, and they must have a list of every one of them themselves.
They have not.

That is peculiar, because the minister recommends a superannuation, and it then goes to the commission, from them to the Treasury board, and from them to council. It is no trouble to get the last, but I am surprised the commission would not have it.

I notice the addition of another solicitor. I know a demand wias made not very long ago to get rid of all these law branches in the different departments, and have all their legal work attended to by the Justice department. Apparently the minister is proceeding in the opposite direction. He is adding to the legal staff. It would look to me a retrograde step.

I do not shore any hon. friend's opinion. Here is a department which
stands by itself, so far as legal work is concerned. We have all sorts of legal cases cropping up in connection with the seizure of stills, automobiles and smuggled goods. We have more legal work to dio than any department outside of the Justice department, and these legal details have to be dealt with in the department before the case is handed over to the Justice department. We have always had one departmental solicitor and one junior departmental solicitor. Until the work began to be as heavy as it is now, we thought we could do without further assistance, but on account of the increase in the work we found it was a great handicap.

I am afraid the hon.
minister does not make many seizures. The door is wide open apparently.

The hon. gentleman's understanding is not absolutely correct. There is smuggling going on. I do not believe that any human being could stop it. You can decrease it and do the best you can. We have made lots of seizures-more than ever before.
Of liquor?

Liquor and cigarettesseizures of smuggled goods and of illicit distilleries and all these things which are carried on in violation of the Inland Revenue Act. Wherever we have been able to find these things we have made a seizure.

Just in line with the
suggestion made by the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) as to a list of those superannuated from this department during the year, I would like also if the minister would supply us with a list of those, if there are any, who have been superannuated and re-employed after being superannuated. I see in the last Auditor General's report a statement made that persons employed in some of the departments have been re-employed after they have been superannuated. I do not think it is a sound practice, if it is being done. The Auditor General's report would indicate it has been done in some cases. I would like to know if it has been done in this department, and I will inquire as to other departments when they come up.
I have been informed that there have been no cases of this kind in the Department of Customs and Excise.
Item agreed to.
Marine and Fisheries-salaries, $484,720.

This proceeding is not
justified. The idea of the rule which provides

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
that the estimates of any department must be opened first on a Monday, Tuesday or Wednesday is to give any member of the House an opportunity of moving a general amendment in criticism of the item, or in reference in some way to that department. Now if the practice which was adopted the other night is to be followed again, of a minister coming in and putting through one item, retiring from the scene, and another minister coming on and putting through another item, of course there is no opportunity for amendment or criticism and the purpose of the rule is gone. What I mean is this; on a Monday, Wednesday or Friday the committee should rise before any minister goes on with his estimates, so that this opportunity of amendment can be given. In a word, if a minister enters upon his estimates, he ought to proceed with them, and the committee should not go from one department to another, thus depriving members of an opportunity of moving an amendment.

I do not think the Prime Minister wants this item called at all. I asked him the idea of going into committee, and unless my ears failed me he told me it was to open the estimates of the Minister of Customs and Excise; because if he did not introduce them to-night he could not go into them later on in the week. Therefore I waived all. objections.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It is quite true, I mentioned that we wished to open the estimates of the Minister of Customs and Excise to-night. What I would like to draw the attention of the House to is that last night it was stated that we would endeavour to take up some estimates both of the Department of Customs and of the Department of Marine and Fisheries. I agree with what the right hon. leader of the opposition states about going from one department to another, if the work of tihe session is at all advanced. I think my hon. friend will understand that unless we take up certain departments Monday, Tuesday or Wednesday, it limits us, because we cannot discuss any estimates on Thursday or Friday that have not been opened on previous days. The Postmaster General will not be here on Friday, and unless we take up these estimates to-night, then the estimates of the Minister of Agriculture would be the only estimates that could be taken up later on in the week.
There are three departments in already.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The estimates of the Minister of Customs have come up to-

night. I think if the hon. leader of the opposition will allow us to call the one item of the estimates of the Department of Marine and Fisheries it would1 facilitate matters. We will not proceed with it.
If it is only for the purpose of enabling the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to come in on Thursday and Friday, I do not object.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is all.
Then I do not object to it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The item before the
committee is item 24, Marine and Fisheries, Salaries, $484,720. Shall I report progress?
Progress reported.
